text:
The air in the family’s hardware store was thick with the scent of sawdust and stale coffee, a sharp contrast to the turpentine and linseed oil that clung to Liam’s clothes. He stood behind the counter, his hands stained not with grease, but with Phthalo Blue, a color that seemed to mock the beige drabness of the inventory list in front of him. His father, Arthur, slammed a ledger onto the counter, the sound echoing like a gunshot in the quiet aisle. "The quarterly reports are down, Liam. Again. You’re spending more time in that studio than you are here, and I’m not paying for a hobby."

Liam’s jaw tightened. "It’s not a hobby, Dad. It’s my life. And if you’d just look at the portfolio I sent you, you’d see—"

"I don’t care about your pictures," Arthur interrupted, his voice dropping to a dangerous whisper. "I care about this business. It’s been in our family for three generations. You think you can just walk away? You think the world will feed you because you’re 'gifted'?"

The tension in the room spiked, suffocating and heavy. Liam wanted to scream, to throw his brushes at the shelves of nails and screws, but he held his ground. "I’m not walking away from you. I’m walking toward who I am. But if you force me to choose between this store and my art, you’re forcing me to choose between my soul and my duty."

Arthur’s eyes hardened, the rift between them widening into a chasm. "Then you’ve already made your choice. Don’t expect me to support a failure."

As Liam turned to leave, his hand brushed against a jar of white granules on a nearby shelf—a remnant of a customer’s request for baking supplies. He paused, fingers lingering on the cool glass. Sugar. It was simple, crystalline, and deceptive. On the tongue, it was a burst of immediate, unadulterated sweetness, a quick fix that satisfied the craving without nourishing the body. It dissolved instantly, leaving no trace, much like the fleeting validation Liam sought from his father’s approval. But sugar also rotted teeth and fueled decay; it was a comfort that ultimately destroyed. Liam looked at the jar, then at his father’s back, and realized their relationship had become like that sweetness: a temporary, cloying comfort that masked a deeper, structural rot
